title: Weathering Effects and Reactivity Restoration in BOF Slag for Use as a Sustainable Binder
abstract: Abstract The valorization of basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag as a binder offers a promising route to reduce the material and energy footprint of the steel and building sector. However, the reactivity of BOF slag is still poorly understood and highly variable. Even small amounts of moisture and carbonation can severely inhibit its hydraulic activity. This study examines three slags (K2, WK2, K3) with varying lime contents and storage histories. The influence of oven drying (40 and 105 °C), controlled rewetting (0.5–1 wt.% water), and milling with triisopropanolamine (TIPA, 0.05 wt.%) on the slag reactivity is investigated in addition to citrate activation. The results are analyzed by isothermal calorimetry, XRD, TGA, and SEM after 3 days. Results show that drying restores reactivity in weathered slags, originally containing 0.64 and 0.91% moisture; a process that can be reversed by rewetting the slags, although there seems to be an optimum moisture content. TIPA promotes hydration in low-lime slag but is insufficient for high-lime slag. These findings stress the critical role of storage and pre-treatment in enabling BOF slag to serve as a consistent sustainable binder. Graphical Abstract

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The building sector is widely recognized as the biggest consumer of raw materials and energy, and as one of the major contributors to global anthropogenic CO 2  emissions. This is primarily due to the extremely high demand for cement, which is produced in quantities exceeding four billion tonnes per year [ 1 ]. Cement production is an energy-intensive process which alone accounts for a large share of process-related CO 2  emissions [ 1 ]. Together, these factors make the cement industry responsible for approximately 7–8% of global emissions [ 1 ,  2 ]. Mitigating the environmental impact of the construction industry therefore requires urgent measures to reduce clinker consumption and to replace Portland cement, either partially or completely, with alternative binders [ 3 ].

One of the most promising approaches is the valorization of industrial by-products and waste as supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) or even as primary binders [ 4 ]. Over the past decades, materials such as coal fly ash, blast furnace slag, and silica fume have been widely studied and, in some cases, successfully implemented in practice [ 5 ,  6 – 7 ]. Among the new promising material, basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag represents a large-volume by-product that is currently underutilized, with most of it ending up in stockpiles or low-value applications such as road base and aggregates [ 8 ,  9 – 10 ]. The reuse of BOF slag in cementitious systems could thus simultaneously reduce waste, lower the demand for clinker, and contribute to circular economy strategies in the steel and construction sectors.

Its chemical composition is comparable to the one of Portland cement, typically containing 30–50% CaO, 10–20% SiO 2 , 20–40% Fe 2 O 3 , and 4–10% MgO, together with smaller amounts of Al 2 O 3 , P 2 O 5 , MnO, and TiO 2  [ 8 ,  11 ,  12 – 13 ]. Its mineralogical composition is dominated by dicalcium silicate (C 2 S), brownmillerite (C 4 AF), and wuestite, together with variable but sometimes significant amounts of free lime (f-CaO) [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ]. Combining the hydraulic reactivity and high availability makes BOF slag a strong candidate for valorization as a binder.

Despite this potential, the large-scale use of BOF slag in cementitious systems remains limited, primarily due to its variable and often insufficient reactivity [ 9 ,  10 ,  17 ]. Activators such as oxalates, phosphates, and potassium citrate have been shown to promote early dissolution of reactive phases and accelerate hydration kinetics, sometimes leading to significant strength gain [ 12 ,  13 ,  15 ,  16 ,  18 ,  19 ]. Tri-potassium citrate has been reported to improve the reactivity of relatively fresh slags by promoting brownmillerite dissolution and hydrogarnets [ 12 ,  13 ,  15 ,  16 ]. However, these strategies may not be sufficient for slags that have already undergone extensive weathering during outdoor storage. One potential reason is weathering reactions driven by moisture and atmospheric CO 2  [ 8 ,  20 ]. These processes result in hydration and carbonation, leading to the formation of portlandite, calcium carbonates, and hydrates at the particle surface [ 21 ,  22 ]. Compared with ordinary Portland cement (OPC), this weathering effect can be particularly detrimental for BOF slag. In OPC, pre-hydration and carbonation typically result in moderate performance reductions [ 22 ,  23 ], but in BOF slag, the combination of relatively low intrinsic reactivity and high f-CaO content may be even more impacted. Free lime hydrates and carbonates much more rapidly than silicate or ferrite phases, leading to the rapid consumption of reactive Ca-bearing species during storage [ 24 ]. The premature formation of portlandite and calcium carbonates may create passivating layers that hinder further dissolution of reactive minerals such as C 2 S and brownmillerite once the slag is used as a binder therefore reducing the capacity of the slag to react. In such cases, even good activators may struggle to overcome the effect of weathering. Addressing this challenge requires not only chemical activation but also a deeper understanding of how storage-induced weathering impacts slag reactivity, and how suitable pre-treatments might restore performance.

To address this gap the present work investigates the impact of weathering on BOF slag reactivity and evaluating the effectiveness of different pre-treatments, such as drying prior to milling or the use of grinding aids. Three slags with different free lime contents and storage histories were selected: K2 (low lime, well stored, non-weathered), WK2 (low lime, weathered outdoors), and K3 (higher lime, weathered outdoors). By performing calorimetry, XRD, TGA and SEM, this study aims to: (1) Identify the weathering products present in BOF slag and assess their influence on the reactivity; (2) Investigate the effect of pre-treatment on reactivity; (3) Relate hydration kinetics to hydrate assemblage and microstructural development.

Through this comprehensive approach, the study provides new insights into the mechanisms limiting BOF slag reactivity and offers practical guidance on storage and processing strategies to enable its use as a reliable major component in low-carbon binders.

sections.heading: Granulometry
paragraphs: The particle size distribution (PSD) of all the samples was measured by laser diffraction spectroscopy using a Mastersizer 2000 (Malvern Instruments). Measurements were carried out in isopropanol dispersion medium to prevent agglomeration. Each reported PSD represents the average of three consecutive measurements.

sections.heading: XRF
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the K2 and K3 slags was measured by X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy on fused beads, using an XRF spectrometer from PANalytical (Epsilon 3 range) with the standardless OMNIAN method. The loss/gain on ignition (LOI/GOI) was assessed by heating the sample in an oven at 1000 °C for 8 h.

sections.heading: XRD
paragraphs: The mineralogical composition of the raw materials and hydrated pastes was characterized by quantitative X-ray diffraction (Q-XRD). The sample powder was inter-milled with 10% pure silica as an internal standard to quantify the amorphous content and then backloaded into the sample holder to minimize preferred orientation effects. The diffraction patterns were collected using a D6 Phaser diffractometer (Bruker) with Co K α  radiation ( λ  = 1.67 Å), a step size of 0.014° 2 θ , and a counting time of 1 s per step, over the 2 θ  range of 11°–90°. Phase quantification was performed with the Rietveld method using TOPAS Academic v5.0 software. The structural data of the different crystalline phases used for refinement are reported in Table  1 . Q-XRD measurements were performed once per sample. An estimation of the error associated with phase consumption and hydration products formation between 0 and 3 days was made based on magnetite variation over this time frame, which is largely considered inert [ 13 ,  15 ,  16 ,  25 ,  26 ]. This error corresponds to the absolute variation in magnetite content between 0 and 3 days, which ranges from 0.1 to 1 wt.% across all samples. Phase consumption was therefore quantified by comparing each hydrated sample (3d) with its corresponding unhydrated sample (0d), and these relative changes were used for correlation with the calorimetry results. sections.heading: TGA
paragraphs: To assess the changes in the hydrate assemblage of the hydrated samples and the possible changes during drying/moisturizing treatment of the raw BOF slags, thermogravimetry analysis (TGA) were performed. The mass losses were recorded by a Netzsch simultaneous analyser (STA 449C) with a heating rate of 10 °C/min, from a temperature of 40–1000 °C. Nitrogen atmosphere was applied in the measuring chamber to avoid a mass increase due to iron oxidation. Around 100 mg of powder was used. For the unhydrated (0 day) samples, measurements were performed in triplicate for each condition to assess reproducibility and variability of the pre-treatment effects. For the hydrated samples after 3 days, TGA measurements were performed twice depending on the pre-treatment; these results are therefore interpreted as indicative trends and are discussed in combination with calorimetry and XRD results.

sections.heading: SEM
paragraphs: Unreacted slag samples were investigated by SEM. Coarse grains were observed before milling, while fine powders were examined after milling. The samples were mounted on carbon tape and sputter-coated with a thin gold layer to ensure conductivity. Imaging was carried out using a Phenom ProX SEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 15 kV. Backscattered electron (BSE) mode was used to generate greyscale images with 256 intensity levels (0 = black, 255 = white), providing contrast based on phase composition.

sections.heading: Calorimetry
paragraphs: Isothermal calorimetry at 20 °C was performed using an I-Cal Ultra from Calmetrix, to characterize the hydration kinetics of the BOF slags activated with 1 wt.% tri-potassium citrate. The activator solution was prepared in advance and mixed with the BOF slag powder on a vibratory mixing table to ensure homogeneity. The water-to-binder ratio (w/b) was kept at 0.18 for all samples. The pastes were loaded into the calorimeter immediately after mixing, and both the heat flow and cumulative heat release were recorded over a period of 3 days. All calorimetry measurements were performed in 3 replicates using independently prepared samples. The reported heat flow and cumulative heat curves correspond to the average of two to three independent measurements.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The selected BOF slags were provided by TATA steel IJmuiden (The Netherlands). They are divided into two categories, class 2 (K2) and class 3 (K3) after production based on their free-lime content, 1–2% and > 3% respectively. All were received in a size fraction of 2–4 mm. K2 slag therefore contains almost no free lime and was stored in airtight containers to avoid weathering for prior research purposes. WK2 is a second batch of class 2 BOF slag that was stored outside, while K3 contains a higher amount of free lime and was stored outside similarly to WK2. The moisture content induced by the storage conditions was assessed on five samples of each slag to identify the extent of weathering. After 48 h of drying at 105 °C, the K2, WK2 and K3 slags average mass loss is 0.16 (± 0.03), 0.63 (± 0.03) and 0.91 (± 0.04) % of their respective mass.

Their chemical composition was determined by X-Ray fluorescence and is presented in Table  2 . The three slags show a very similar oxide composition all being mostly composed of calcium oxide, iron oxide and silicon oxide representing around 39, 31 and 12 wt.%, respectively. Minor oxides present are magnesium, manganese and aluminum oxide as well as a small amount of heavy metals such as chromium and vanadium (< 0.5%). Table 2 Chemical composition of BOF slags Oxides (wt.%) K2 WK2 K3 CaO 38.2 38.2 40.0 Fe 2 O 3 a 30.6 31.7 32.4 SiO 2 12.6 12.6 12.6 MgO 8.4 7.6 7.0 MnO 4.2 4.3 4.0 Al 2 O 3 1.7 1.7 2.0 TiO 2 1.3 1.4 1.2 P 2 O 5 1.2 1.2 1.2 V 2 O 5 1.3 1.1 1.0 Cr 2 O 3 0.3 0.2 0.3 Na 2 O 0.1 0.0 0.1 GOI b 0.2 – – LOI c – 0.3 0.4 a Iron oxide is reported as Fe 2 O 3 , despite the well known presence of FeO, with a Fe2O3/FeO found to be around 0.25 [ 39 ] b GOI: Gain on ignition c  LOI: Loss on ignition, corresponding to the mass gain or loss in the samples heated up to 1000 °C. Loss is attributed to the loss of volatile components, gain is attributed to oxidation of FeO

The X-ray diffraction patterns of the BOF slags are shown in Fig.  1  and the corresponding quantification results are reported in Table  3 . The three BOF slags are mainly composed of C 2 S (Ca 2 SiO 4 , ICSD 81097) (44–51 wt.%), brownmillerite (Ca 2 (Al,Fe) 2 O 5 , PDF 04-014-6627) (16–18 wt.%) and wuestite ((Mg,(Fe)O), ICSD 67200) (20–22 wt.%) as primary minerals, present in very similar quantities in all slags. The free lime (f-CaO, ICSD 28905) content ranges from very low (0.4 and 0.8%) in K2 and WK2 to higher (1.9%) in K3, in agreement with supplier information. In addition to f-CaO K3 also contains 1.5 wt.% of portlandite (Ca(OH) 2 , PDF 01-076-0571), most likely due to the weathering of K3 and the rapid conversion of f-CaO to calcium hydroxide [ 24 ]. In WK2, 0.4 wt.% of portlandite is found, for the same reason, however the amount remains low due to the initial very low amount of free lime. Additionally, a certain amorphous content is quantified for each slag and accounts for 18, 10 and 20 wt.% in K2, WK2, and K3, respectively. Part of the amorphous content is likely due to the presence of amorphous hydration products in WK2 and K3 as the presence of portlandite suggests prior hydration. A part of the amorphous content in slag is also due to X-Ray amorphization of primary minerals during milling, especially in K2 [ 14 ,  16 ,  18 ]. Hydrogarnets (Ca 3 (Al,Fe) 2 (SiO 4 )(OH) 4 , ICSD 66274) and pyroaurite (Mg 6 Fe 2 CO 3 (OH) 16 .4H 2 O, PDF 01-074-1513) were not clearly identified, in agreement with literature [ 14 ,  15 ,  19 ,  26 ], and the calcite (CaCO 3 , ICSD 80869) amount detected (~ 1%) is very similar for all three. Fig. 1 XRD patterns of the BOF slag as received (B = Brownmillerite, W = Wuestite, M = Magnetite, C2S, P = Portlandite, C = Calcite, Hg = Hydrogarnets, PA = Pyroaurite) Table 3 Quantified phases in the raw BOF slags Phases (wt.%) K2 W-K2 K3 Brownmillerite 14.5 18.1 17.1 C 2 S 35.4 37.0 31.7 Wuestite 23.7 24.9 21.4 Magnetite 5.9 7.4 4.8 Free lime 0.4 0.8 1.9 Portlandite 0.5 0.6 1.5 Hydrogarnets 0.0 0.0 0.0 Pyroaurite 0.0 0.0 0.0 Calcite 0.7 1.1 1.2 Amorphous 18.9 10.1 20.3

Thermogravimetric analysis was performed on all the raw BOF slags to double check XRD data and the TG and DTG curves are presented in Fig.  2 . The samples were vacuum dried at ambient temperature for 24 h to remove free water. For BOF slag the mass loss can be attributed to C–S–H, pyroaurite, hydrogarnets, portlandite and calcium carbonates [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 – 16 ,  18 ] in the specific temperature ranges, 40–200 °C for C–S–H [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 – 30 ]and pyroaurite dehydration [ 30 ,  31 ,  32 ,  33 – 34 ], 200–400 °C for the water loss of hydrogarnets [ 30 ,  35 ,  36 ], ~ 450 °C for portlandite [ 24 ,  30 ] and 600–850 °C for CO 2  from pyroaurite and calcium carbonates [ 30 ,  33 ,  34 ,  37 ,  38 ]. The overall mass loss of the three BOF slag is 0.69 ± 0.05, 2.63 ± 0.22, and 3.18 ± 0.04% for K2, WK2 and K3, respectively. The difference between these values and the LOI values that are lower is likely due to the oxidation of iron in air atmosphere (LOI) that is not occurring under inert atmosphere (TGA), [ 39 ]. In K2 the small mass loss is mostly due to a loss in the 600–800 °C temperature range attributed to the decomposition of calcium carbonates as confirmed by XRD data. Two very small peaks can be observed in the range of C–S–H and hydrogarnets, respectively, but remain extremely small. For WK2, a similar mass loss is observed due to calcium carbonates, nevertheless a bigger loss associated with C–S–H and hydrogarnets is found. Additionally, a small, distinct peak is observed around 450 °C that can be attributed to portlandite dehydration. The K3 slag shows a higher amount of portlandite compared to WK2 while a similar mass loss is found for C–S–H, hydrogarnets and calcium carbonates. Overall, these results are in good agreement with the quantitative XRD data and confirm the presence of hydration products already present in the WK2 and K3 slag. They will be referred to a pre-hydration product to differentiate them from the reaction products of BOF slag with citrate. Fig. 2 Thermogravimetric analysis of the raw BOF slags ( a  Mass loss;  b  Dtg curves)

SEM observations of the raw (2–4 mm sized, untreated) slags highlight clear contrasts in the extent of weathering among K2, WK2, and K3 (Fig.  3 ). K2 grains appear angular, with sharp crystalline surfaces and traces of carbonates, in agreement with TG. In contrast, WK2 grains exhibit extensive surface coverage by secondary products that are likely calcite and other hydration product. K3 grains are dominated by large, plate-like portlandite crystals, often accompanied by carbonate clusters. This morphology agrees with the strong portlandite decomposition peak observed in TG. Fig. 3 SEM micrographs of BOF slag grains investigated, untreated, and unmilled: images  a ,  d ,  g  show K2;  b ,  e ,  h  show WK2;  c ,  f ,  i  show K3, from lower to higher magnification, respectively

Prior to reactivity testing, all BOF slags were milled from 2 to 4 mm size fraction to fine powder with the same procedure (described in Section “ Milling ”) The PSDs of the three BOF slags reported in Fig.  4 , are very similar, with d 50  ranging from 6.5 to 10 µm, which minimizes reactivity variations due to particle size. The powders were mixed with a solution of tri-potassium citrate (0.19 M) with a  w / b  of 0.18 and loaded into the calorimeter at 20 °C, for 3 days measurements. The calorimetric curves are presented in Fig.  5 . It can be clearly seen that only K2 releases heat (47.4 ± 0.1 J/g) and starts reacting after 10 h of induction period. The weathered slags show no sign of reactivity and almost no heat is recorded after 3 days of measurement. From this observation, it can be hypothesized that the reactivity of the weathered slags was inhibited due to the weathering layer on the grains. Fig. 4 Particle size distribution of the raw BOF slag after milling ( a  volume distribution;  b  cumulative volume) Fig. 5 Reactivity of the BOF slag milled as received and mixed with a solution of 0.19 M of tri-potassium citrate (w/b = 0.18) ( a  heat flow curves;  b  total heat released curves)

Although the three BOF slags showed very similar bulk chemical and mineralogical compositions based on XRF and quantitative XRD analyses, differences in storage conditions resulted in different degrees of weathering. Small variations in free lime content and amorphous fraction were observed, together with the presence of pre-hydration products such as portlandite in WK2 and K3. Weathering during outdoor storage led to partial hydration and carbonation of reactive phases and the formation of secondary products at the surface of the slag grains, as confirmed by TG and SEM observations. These differences, while limited in terms of overall phase abundance, affected the initial state of the slags prior to reactivity testing and were therefore considered when interpreting the hydraulic behavior of the materials.

sections.heading: Pretreatments
paragraphs: Several pre-treatments were applied to the slags before or during milling (from 2 to 4 mm size fraction to fine powder) in order to restore the reactivity of the inhibited slags and understand what mechanism is killing the reactivity.

sections.heading: Drying
paragraphs: Prior to milling, the slags were oven dried for 48 h. The slags were spread in a 3 cm-thick layer in buckets and placed in an oven with ventilation. Two temperatures were tested, 40 and 105 °C. The resulting samples are named, K2 40, K2 105, WK2 40, WK2 105, K3 40 and K3 105.

sections.heading: Grinding Aids
paragraphs: Tri isopropanol amine (TIPA) was also used to facilitate the milling of the weathered slag [ 19 ,  40 ] and investigate if it can restore their reactivity. An amount of 0.05% were mixed to WK2 and K3 just before milling.

sections.heading: Rewetting
paragraphs: To understand the impact of moisture on the reactivity, the dried slags (105 °C) were rewetted by spraying 0.5 or 1 wt.% of water onto a 3 cm-thick layer of each BOF slag. The samples were then homogenized and stayed in closed airtight containers for one week before milling.

sections.heading: Milling
paragraphs: Each slag (2–4 mm size fraction), weathered or un-weathered, was milled for 30 min in a planetary ball mill (Pulverisette 5, Retsch) using steel milling jars and steel balls at a rotational speed of 250 rpm. To limit an increase of the temperature during milling, an intermittent milling protocol was applied, consisting of alternating cycles of 2 min milling and 2 min pause, based on preliminary tests. The ball charge (25 balls, 20 mm diameter) and jar volume (500 mL) were fixed for all experiments, while the powder charge was fixed by volume (250 mL), resulting in a constant total filling degree of approximately 71 vol.%. Consequently, the powder mass varied between 350 and 400 g depending on the slag, leading to a ball-to-powder ratio ranging from approximately 2.05 to 2.34 by mass. The volume distributions and cumulative volume curves are presented for raw slags and each type of pre-treatment in Figs.  6 ,  7 , and  8 . All powders are very fine with, d 50  ranging from 6.08 to 15.04 µm. The different treatments are slightly modifying the PSDs, particularly rewetting (0.5 and 1%) slightly increases the overall PSD of the three BOF slags, however drying of the raw slags and milling with grinding aids do not significantly reduce or even change the PSD. In general, no correlation between the PSD and the hydration kinetics (presented in this work) is found. Fig. 6 Particle size distribution of the dried BOF slag after milling ( a  volume distribution;  b  cumulative volume) Fig. 7 Particle size distribution of the BOF slag milled with TIPA ( a  volume distribution;  b  cumulative volume) Fig. 8 Particle size distribution of the rewetted BOF slag after milling ( a  volume distribution;  b  cumulative volume)

sections.heading: Effect of Drying Treatment
paragraphs: Figure  9  presents the heat flow and cumulative heat curves of K2 (Fig.  9 a, d), WK2 (Fig.  9 b, e), and K3 (Fig.  9 c, f) slags, both untreated and dried at 40 °C and 105 °C, after activation with tri-potassium citrate. Their starting moisture content was 0.16, 0.64 and 0.91, respectively. In Fig.  9 a, d,  K2  (un-dried) exhibits the highest reactivity, with a short induction period (10 h) followed by a sharp main peak and a cumulative heat release of around 47.4 ± 0.06 J/g after 3 days. Interestingly, drying at 40 °C and 105 °C slightly delays the main hydration peak by 2 and 5 h, respectively. The cumulative heat of K2 40 is, however, almost the same (48.2 ± 0.3 J/g), while that of K2 105 is reduced (36.2 ± 1.1 J/g). In contrast, WK2 (Fig.  9 b, e) and K3 (Fig.  9 c, f) (both weathered slags) show negligible reactivity when untreated, with almost no heat release (8.2 ± 0.3 and 2.3 ± 0.3 J/g). After drying, however, both recover their reactivity. The effect is most pronounced at 40 °C, where the main peak is restored and the cumulative heat reaches 53.5 ± 1.2 J/g for WK2 and 59.3 ± 0.8 J/g for K3. Drying at 105 °C not only improves the heat flow maximum for the WK2 sample but also delays it similar to the K2 105. Overall, the total heat is slightly lower heat for WK2 105 (52.3 ± 1.1 J/g) than for WK2 40. Interestingly for K3 105 the heat flow maximum occurs earlier although the overall heat release is much lower (48.2 ± 0.7 J/g). These results suggest that drying mitigates the possible passivation effects caused by pre-hydration and/or carbonation during storage, with moderate drying (40 °C) being particularly effective. It should be noted that the moisture content remains different between those samples with the 40-dried samples still containing 0.05 ± 0.03, 0.23 ± 0.05, and 0.34 ± 0.05 wt.% for K2, WK2, and K3, respectively. The effect of moisture content itself is discussed in Section “ Effect of Moisture Content .” Fig. 9 Hydration kinetics of the samples untreated and dried at 40 and 105 °C ( a ,  b ,  c  heat flow curves of K2, WK2 and K3 samples;  e ,  f  and  g  cumulative heat curves of K2, WK2 and K3 samples)

Figure  10  shows the TG and DTG curves of the untreated and dried slags before hydration (0 day) and after 3 days of hydration. For the unhydrated slags, the main differences lie in the amount of bound water, while carbonate content remains similar between the three. Untreated K2 (Fig.  10 a, d) shows almost no dehydration peaks and a small peak in the range 600–900 °C attributed to calcium carbonate decomposition. In contrast, WK2 (Fig.  10 b, e) and K3 (Fig.  10 c, f) exhibit greater mass loss in the ranges 40–200 °C (C–S–H, pyroaurite), 200–400 °C (hydrogarnets), and 400–540 °C (portlandite), confirming their partial weathering. Additionally, the weight loss attributed to portlandite decomposition is much larger for K3 than for K2, in agreement with the amount of free lime available to form Ca(OH) 2  during storage. The influence of drying on K2 is minimal as the TG and DTG curves are very similar. For WK2, drying at 40 °C does not lead to significant changes, while drying at 105 °C reduces the total mass loss from 2.63 ± 0.22 to 1.81 ± 0.03% due to the disappearance of the C–S–H peak in the range 40–200 °C. This suggests that the C–S–H formed during storage decomposes at 105 °C, while 40 °C allows it to be preserved [ 30 ]. For K3, both temperatures lead to a decrease in mass loss from 3.18 ± 0.04 to 1.91 ± 0.05 and 2.32 ± 0.05%, respectively. Both reduce the mass loss due to C–S–H decomposition and that attributed to portlandite dehydration, while slightly increasing the CO 2  loss. K3 40 shows the smallest portlandite peak, a slightly bigger carbonate peak, and a very small hump in the C–S–H region, while K3 105 shows the total removal of the C–S–H peak, a reduced but still significant portlandite peak, and slightly less carbonate in comparison. After 3 days of hydration, all slags develop additional mass losses between 40 and 400 °C, consistent with the expected formation of C–S–H, hydrogarnets, and possibly pyroaurite [ 15 ,  27 ,  30 ,  33 ]. The amount of carbonates is increased in all hydrated samples and can be attributed to calcium carbonates, pyroaurite decarbonation, and citrate compounds, explaining the large increase. Consistent with calorimetry results, K2 3d, K3 40 3d and K3 105 3d show almost the same TG and DTG curves, confirming the very small impact of drying. In contrast, the effect of drying is high in WK2 and K3: the samples dried at 40 and 105 °C develop significantly higher mass losses than the untreated references, and their DTG curves are very similar to those of the K2 samples. Besides this, drying at 40 °C results in an even higher mass loss than at 105 °C. TG analysis corroborates the calorimetry results by showing the presence of additional bound water and carbonates after 3 days, confirming ongoing reactions. Fig. 10 Thermogravimetric analysis of the samples untreated and dried raw (0d) and hydrated for 3d with tri-potassium citrate ( a ,  b ,  c  TG curves of K2, WK2, and K3 samples;  e ,  d  and  f  DTG curves of K2, WK2, and K3 samples)

Table  4  shows the XRD quantification of the untreated and dried slags at 0 and 3 days. The main crystalline phases are C 2 S (larnite,  α  and  α ′ polymorphs), brownmillerite, and wuestite, with magnetite and minor free lime also present. Drying has no major effect on these primary phases, confirming that their stability is unaffected by moderate heating. Instead, differences appear in the amorphous and secondary products. For K2, the amorphous content decreases from 19 wt.% (untreated) to 14 wt.% (40 °C dried) and 11 wt.% (105 °C dried). For K3, the amorphous content stays the same after drying at 40 °C (20 wt.%), while it decreases after drying at 105 °C to 14 wt.%. In WK2, a sharp increase after drying at 40 °C is observed (from 10 to 17 wt.%), while the amount of amorphous drops in WK2 105 (7 wt.%). No crystalline hydration products are detected, however, portlandite and calcite are present, with the portlandite amount in good agreement with the TG peaks around 450 °C, while the calcite amount stays around 1 wt.% in all the samples and therefore hardly correlates with the carbonate amounts detected with TGA. Mostly due to the CO 2  loss from pyroaurite, citrate compounds and other carbonates polymorphs on top of calcite [ 15 ]. After 3 days of hydration, quantification shows primarily a decrease in brownmillerite content in the K2 pastes and the dried WK2 and K3, confirming their reactivity. C 2 S and wuestite do not significantly decrease, which is expected in the first 3 days of hydration, as wuestite is not very reactive and C 2 S only at later ages [ 14 ,  15 – 16 ]. Almost no hydrogarnets and pyroaurite are present; where detected (K2 40, K2 105), they stayed below 1 wt.%. Their absence might be due to their low crystallinity at 3 days, as confirmed with TGA. Portlandite content is similar to that of the unreacted samples, consistently with TGA results. The calcite amount also stays stable, in contrast to the TG results, suggesting that the CO 2  loss in the hydrated samples is not only due to calcite decomposition but also other phases containing CO2 such as pyroaurite (probably X-ray amorphous), and citrate compounds. The biggest changes at 3 days occurs in the amorphous content, which increases significantly in most of the samples, suggesting the formation of amorphous hydration products (C–S–H gel, hydrogarnets, pyroaurite). Consistently, the amorphous content stays unchanged in the WK2 and K3 weathered slags at 3 days compared to 0 day. It should be noted that the only reactive sample that exhibits a reduction of amorphous content after 3 days (19 to 13.5 wt.%) is K2, which is consistent with other studies on this specific BOF slag, showing a reduction of amorphous content at early ages before an increase at later ages [ 14 ,  16 ]. This is reported to be possibly due to the amorphization of C 2 S or other primary minerals during milling, which can further react at early age [ 14 ,  16 ,  41 ].

Overall, the calorimetry, TG, and XRD results clearly demonstrate that drying strongly influences the reactivity of BOF slags, especially those affected by weathering. Drying at 40 °C restores reactivity by possibly removing part of the moisture and weakening poorly crystalline hydrates, while not completely damaging already present C–S–H gel, which in contrast to portlandite and calcium carbonates may promote hydration [ 24 ,  42 ]. When applying stronger drying (105 °C), reactivity is also restored in the case of weathered slags; nevertheless, reactivity remains lower and is significantly delayed in the case of the non-weathered slags.

Drying at 40 °C appears to be the most suitable pre-treatment condition, as it consistently restores the reactivity of the weathered slags (WK2 and K3) and leads to the highest cumulative heat release. In contrast, drying at 105 °C results in delayed hydration and lower total heat released, particularly for K2 and K3. Overall, the combined calorimetry, TGA, and XRD results indicate that moderate drying is sufficient to mitigate surface passivation while preserving a favorable phase assemblage. Drying at 40 °C preserves or increases the amorphous content in the weathered slags, whereas drying at 105 °C is associated with a reduction of this fraction, particularly in WK2 and K3. These trends are accompanied by differences in hydration kinetics and total heat released. This may suggest a possible link between the amorphous fraction and early-age reactivity. From an industrial perspective, drying at 40 °C offers clear advantages, as it reduces energy demand compared to higher-temperature treatments. Importantly, reactivity recovery at 40 °C is obtained without requiring longer milling times or more intensive grinding conditions, making this pretreatment more compatible with existing industrial processing routes and more attractive in terms of energy efficiency and operational cost.

sections.heading: Effect of Grinding Aid
paragraphs: Figure  11  shows the hydration kinetics of WK2 (Fig.  11 a) and K3 (Fig.  11 b) slags milled with 0.05 wt.% TIPA compared to the untreated samples. WK2, which was initially unreactive, exhibits a clear reactivation when milled with TIPA. The heat flow curve displays a distinct main peak starting at around 20 h, leading to a cumulative heat released above 40 ± J/g after 3 days. This demonstrates that TIPA effectively restores the reactivity of the weathered WK2 slag, most likely by improving surface conditions and enhancing dissolution of the reactive phases [ 19 ,  40 ,  43 ,  44 ]. By contrast, K3 shows little response to TIPA addition. Both the heat flow and cumulative heat curves remain very low, with only a slight increase compared to the untreated slag (7 to 10 J/g). This indicates that TIPA cannot overcome the strong passivation observed in K3, which can be due to the higher free lime content and the predominance of portlandite/carbonates inhibiting phase dissolution. Fig. 11 Hydration kinetics of the samples untreated and milled with 0.05 wt.% TIPA ( a  heat flow curves;  b  cumulative heat curves)

The effect of TIPA is further supported by thermogravimetric analysis in Fig.  12 . The samples at 0 day show an increased mass loss in the samples milled with TIPA compared to the untreated slags. For both WK2 (Fig.  12 a, c) and K3 (Fig.  12 b, d) three peaks appear one for C–S–H, one for hydrogarnets even though very small and one for portlandite which is more pronounced for K3. After 3 days, WK2 TIPA shows significant additional mass losses compared to untreated ones, particularly in the ranges 40–200 °C and 200–400 °C, which can be attributed to the formation of C–S–H gel, hydrogarnets and pyroaurite, confirming the progress of hydration, the peak attributed to hydrogarnets is particularly distinct compared to other slags previously observed, this may indicate that TIPA-milling may also activate brownmillerite as reported by Zepper et al. [ 18 ].Surprisingly, the 3-day hydrated K3 TIPA sample shows similar Dtg curve with a less pronounced peak for hydrogarnets and a clearer peak for portlandite. The overall mass loss is lower than for WK2 TIPA, however it is not consistent with the calorimetry results. Fig. 12 Thermogravimetric analysis of the samples untreated and milled with TIPA (0d) and hydrated for 3d with tri-potassium citrate ( a ,  b  TG curves of WK2 and K3 samples;  c ,  d  DTG curves of WK2 and K3 samples)

These observations are corroborated by the XRD results reported in Table  5 . In WK2, milling with TIPA reduces the content of brownmillerite and C 2 S polymorphs after 3 days, while simultaneously increasing the amorphous fraction (from 10.2 to 19.2 wt.%) and leading to the appearance of hydrogarnets (3.6 wt.%) and hydrotalcite (1.6 wt.%). These changes confirm the precipitation of new hydrates and validate the reactivation of this slag with highlighting the beneficial effect of alkanolamine such as TIPA to activate brownmillerite [ 19 ,  40 ,  44 ]. Conversely, in K3, the consumption of reactive minerals is limited, with Brownmillerite, C 2 S and wuestite staying stable within the error. The amorphous content decreases after 3 days of hydration (17–12 wt.%). However, hydrogarnets and pyroaurite are detected similarly in smaller amount than in WK2, this is in good agreement with TGA results but however still surprising considering calorimetry results. In summary, TIPA has a strong positive effect on the reactivity of weathered K2 slag, enabling renewed hydration and hydrate precipitation, but it fails to restore hydration in K3. The contrast between these two slags suggests that the effectiveness of grinding aids depends strongly on the initial mineralogy and degree of weathering of the slag. Nevertheless, the investigated phase assemblage of K3 TIPA sample contradicts the calorimetry results. As previously demonstrated the early heat released from citrate-activated BOF slag paste is strongly related with the formation of hydrogarnets. The hydration products detected with TGA are probably formed after 60 h of hydration, based on the calorimetry results, however the mass loss associated is still surprisingly high. One hypothesis can be the composition and structure of very recently formed hydrates that may also contains more bound water than older ones. Nevertheless, this results also demonstrates that TIPA helps to restore also the reactivity of K3 but with a very significant delay in the hydration compared to WK2.

Overall, these results show that TIPA-assisted grinding can effectively restore the reactivity of weathered BOF slag when passivation is moderate, as observed for WK2. In this case, the combined calorimetry, TGA, and XRD data indicate enhanced dissolution of reactive phases and the formation of new hydration products, including hydrogarnets and an increased amorphous fraction. In contrast, TIPA has a limited effect on K3, where the higher free lime content and the predominance of portlandite and carbonates appear to maintain a strong surface passivation that cannot be efficiently overcome by chemical grinding assistance alone. These observations suggest that the efficiency of grinding aids such as TIPA strongly depends on the initial slag chemistry and degree of weathering, and that surface passivation mechanisms play a key role in controlling the hydration response.

sections.heading: Effect of Moisture Content
paragraphs: The effect of controlled rewetting after drying at 105 °C on the reactivity is shown in Fig.  13 . The results reveal that the influence of reintroduced moisture on slag reactivity is highly dependent on the water dosage. For all slags, wetting with 0.5 wt.% water increases its cumulative heat release compared to the dried conditions, reaching the very consistent total heat values of 60.1 (± 1.0), 56,3 (± 1.3), 53.9 (± 1.4) J/g compared to 36.2 (± 1.1), 52.3 (± 1.1), 48.2 (± 0.7) J/g for the dried slags. By contrast, the 1 wt.% rewetting condition is less effective, with delayed and weaker hydration peaks, and lower cumulative heat. The 1% rewetted samples exhibit a total heat released lower (31.3 ± 1.8, 15.9 ± 1.0, 41.3 ± 1.6 J/g) than the dried slags, but still higher than the initial weathered slag. In the case of K3 the total heat is slightly lower mainly due to the delay of the main hydration peak that appears after 20 h compared to the 5 h of the dried K3 (Fig.  13 c, f). The same delay leading to the same decrease in the total heat of hydration is observed for K2 (Fig.  13 a, d). For WK2 (Fig.  13 b, e) the hydration is even more delayed compared to its dried reference, the main peak appearing after 35 h compared to 10 h. Fig. 13 Hydration kinetics of the samples untreated, dried and rewetted with 0.5 and 1% of water ( a ,  b ,  c  heat flow curves of K2, WK2, and K3, respectively;  d ,  e ,  f  cumulative heat curves of K2, WK2, K3, respectively)

The TGA results are presented in Fig.  14 . In the unhydrated samples (0d), it is clearly shown that the rewetted samples have a lower total mass loss than the K2 (Fig.  14 a, d), WK2 (Fig.  14 b, e) and K3 (Fig.  14 c, f) untreated. This is mainly due to the drying step before rewetting that leaded to the total mass loss of 0.47, 1.76, 2.36 for K2 105, WK2 105 and K3 105, respectively. However, it confirms that the short-term exposure to water is not clearly forming hydration products resulting in a mass loss only slightly increased or unchanged within the error, with values of 0.67 and 0.38 for K2, 2.15 and 1.98 for WK2 and 1.76 and 1.47 for K3. However, the mas loss stays lower than the slags in their initial states. After 3 days of hydration the samples demonstrate a larger total mass loss, with a clear difference between the 0.5 and 1% samples. K2, WK2 and K3 0.5% that exhibited the larger total heat released show indeed the greater mass loss, with clear peak attributed to C–S–H water loss, a wide hump for hydrogarnet and a clear peak for portlandite in K3. In contrast the slags rewetted with 1% of water have a mass loss even lower than the untreated slags. Fig. 14 Thermogravimetric analysis of the samples untreated, dried and rewetted with 0.5 and 1% of water ( a ,  b ,  c  TG curves of K2, WK2, and K3 samples, respectively;  d ,  e ,  f  DTG curves of K2, WK2, and K3 samples, respectively)

XRD results reported in Table  6 , support this trend. In all samples the amount of brownmillerite decreases between 0 and 3 days and the amorphous content is going up. C 2 S, and wuestite remain stable, similarly to the other samples (dried, TIPA) as well as the calcite and portlandite amount. Comparably with the dried samples hydrogarnets and pyroaurite are not detected, also due to their possible amorphous state at early age [ 31 ,  36 ,  45 ]. Overall, the water content also influences the phase quantification, and more brownmillerite is consumed, accompanied with a greater increase of the amorphous content in the 0.5% samples. All together, these results indicate that the reintroduction of limited moisture can be beneficial for improving the reactivity of slags. A small water dosage (0.5 wt.%) appears to promote dissolution and hydrate formation. Conversely, slightly higher moisture content (1 wt.%) tends to reduce reactivity.

sections.heading: Discussion and Comparison of Pretreatments
paragraphs: The pre-treatment strategies investigated, drying and milling with a grinding aid (TIPA), show that the reactivity of BOF slags is highly dependent on their weathering state and, to some extent, on their lime content. Even relatively low amounts of weathering can have a strong effect. In addition, controlled rewetting experiments are performed to evaluate the role of moisture content on hydration performance. A comparative analysis reveals both shared mechanisms and key differences in how passivation can be overcome and how moisture modulates hydration.

Drying shows the most straightforward and generally effective approach. Mild drying at 40 °C removes physically adsorbed water and can destabilize poorly crystalline hydrates without altering the reactive phases, thereby restoring or even enhancing hydration kinetics in WK2 and K3. This agrees with previous work showing that weathering products such as Ca(OH) 2  and CaCO 3  form surface passivating layers that block dissolution of reactive minerals [ 21 ,  22 ]. At 105 °C, however, the benefit is less pronounced, particularly for WK2, even if still beneficial. A plausible explanation is that excessive dehydration induces densification or recrystallization of surface products, making them less permeable to dissolution, in line with the behavior of cement hydrates subjected to stronger drying [ 24 ,  46 ]. These results suggest that drying does not remove portlandite or carbonates but weakens their continuity or induces microcracking, thereby exposing fresh reactive surfaces [ 21 ,  22 ].

TIPA addition shows a contrasting effect. In WK2, TIPA restores heat release due to hydrate precipitation comparable to drying. This effect is consistent with the dual role of alkanolamines: improving milling efficiency (dispersion and fineness) and chemically activating brownmillerite by complexing with Fe ions [ 19 ]. In K3, however, TIPA has little impact, suggesting that when passivation layers are dominated by large amount of portlandite and some carbonates—sparingly soluble at high pH (~ 12.5) [ 21 ,  22 ,  47 ,  48 ], chemical assistance during milling seems insufficient to overcome the barrier.

The total heat released is compared to the mass loss recorded with TGA in Fig.  15 . Linear regression analysis is presented between heat and mass loss in specific range. Figure  15 a) shows that the best correlation was obtained between the cumulative heat (3 days) and the total mass loss in the range 40–900 °C ( R 2  = 0.60). This confirms that the overall mass loss that includes both bound water and CO 2 , provides a reliable indicator of hydration extent and correlates well with heat release. When individual components are considered (Fig.  15 b), the best fit is found between hydrogarnets and total heat, confirming that in citrate-activated BOF slag pastes, brownmillerite hydration leading to hydrogarnet formation is the dominant early-age reaction [ 13 ,  14 ]. Fig. 15 Correlation between mass loss and total heat released after 3 days of hydration. The cumulative heat values correspond to the average of replicate calorimetry measurements, with standard deviations ranging from 0.06 to 2.03 J/g depending on the sample ( a  mass loss from C–S–H to total weight loss;  b  mass loss considering mass loss attributed to specific secondary products, 40–200 for C–S–H + pyroaurite, 200–400 for hydrogarnets, 400–530 for portlandite, 540–900 for carbonates)

Phase quantification (Fig.  16 ) shows only limited correlations between phase consumption (a) or hydrate formation (b) and the total heat. For phase consumption, the best fits are obtained for brownmillerite and wuestite, suggesting that higher consumption of these phases corresponds to greater heat release. This result is consistent with their reactivity under citrate activation [ 12 ,  15 ,  16 ]. For hydration products, interpretation is limited by the almost total absence of crystalline hydrates: this makes it difficult to link calorimetry directly to hydrogarnet formation. Instead, the amorphous fraction is the only significant influencing factor. The amount of amorphous phase at 0 day does not appear to control reactivity, but the 3-day values show a positive correlation with total heat ( R 2  ≈ 0.44), which is reasonably strong given the uncertainties in quantifying amorphous and poorly crystalline phases by XRD [ 30 ]. When the difference between 3 and 0 days amorphous content is considered, the correlation becomes weaker. This suggests that pre-formed hydration products do not directly determine reactivity. Fig. 16 Correlation between phase quantifications and total heat released after 3 days of hydration. The cumulative heat values correspond to the average of replicate calorimetry measurements, with standard deviations ranging from ± 0.06 to ± 2.03 J/g depending on the sample ( a  consumed phase,  b  quantified hydration products including hydrogarnets, pyroaurite and amorphous)

Re-exposure to moisture highlights the critical role of water content. Since the slags are already reactive after drying, rewetting is applied to isolate the influence of added water. A clear dosage dependence is observed: at 0.5 wt.% water, both WK2 and K3 show a better reactivity, suggesting that limited moisture may improve surface charge distribution or initial dissolution of ions [ 49 ]. However, at 1 wt.% water the effect is reversed, with slower hydration and lower cumulative heat. Importantly, TG and XRD at 0 day show no significant additional portlandite or carbonate formation compared to the dried slags, and the 0.5 wt.% samples even exhibit slightly higher mass loss than the 1 wt.% samples. This indicates that the reduced reactivity at 1 wt.% moisture is not due to new secondary phases, but rather to the negative influence of excess water itself, for instance, by hindering milling efficiency, causing stronger agglomeration, or altering surface charge conditions unfavorable.

Figure  17  illustrates this relationship between total heat release and residual moisture content. Below a threshold of ~ 0.5–0.6 wt.%, moisture appears beneficial for reactivity, and a decent correlation is observed ( R 2  = 0.61). In contrast, above this level slags become progressively less reactive. This is consistent with the greater reactivity of the samples dried at 40 °C, which retain small amounts of residual moisture (0.04, 0.23, and 0.36 wt.% for K2, WK2, and K3 respectively) compared to the completely dry or over-wetted samples. These observations indicate that drying may restore reactivity mainly by reducing excess water, through modification of surface charge and weakening of the secondary product layer. Fig. 17 Moisture content vs total heat released (the cumulative heat values correspond to the average of replicate calorimetry measurements, with standard deviations ranging from ± 0.06 to ± 2.03 J/g depending on the sample)

The TIPA-milled samples provide an additional nuance. Dissolved in water before milling, TIPA increases the moisture content of WK2 and K3 from 0.64 and 0.91 wt.% to 0.77 and 1.3 wt.% respectively. In line with the above trend, K3 TIPA releases little heat after 3 days, consistent with its higher moisture level. WK2 TIPA, however, is highly reactive. This exception can be attributed to the dual effect of TIPA: facilitating milling even under moist conditions and chemically activating brownmillerite. Taken together, these findings suggest that the detrimental effect of weathering is linked to both moisture content and the presence of pre-formed secondary products (C–S–H, portlandite, carbonates). These phases are not removed by milling and persist as low-solubility coatings, especially at high pH in the citrate-activated system.

From a practical and industrial perspective, the results of this study indicate that pre-treatment strategies for BOF slags should be selected based on both storage conditions and slag composition. Among the investigated approaches, moderate drying at 40 °C appears to be the most robust option for restoring reactivity in weathered slags, particularly for materials with higher free lime content. Given that drying at 40 °C already provides equal or better reactivity recovery compared to drying at 105 °C, increasing the drying temperature does not appear justified. Heating large quantities of slag to higher temperatures leads to substantially higher energy consumption and operating costs. For low lime weathered slags, grinding with TIPA can also effectively restore reactivity and may represent an alternative when drying is not feasible. However, this approach is insufficient for free lime-rich slags, where surface passivation by portlandite dominates and may make TIPA ineffective at this dosage. Overall, these findings show that reactivity restoration can be effectively achieved through tailored pre-treatment strategies guided by basic slag characteristics, such as free lime content, moisture level, and storage history, thereby supporting the development of practical and industrially viable processing routes for BOF slags.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study has shown that the reactivity of BOF slags is strongly impaired by weathering during outdoor storage, yet it can be partially or fully restored through suitable pre-treatments. The effectiveness of these treatments depends not only on the applied method but also on the slag’s intrinsic free lime content and the extent of weathering. By combining calorimetry, XRD, and TGA analyses, the mechanisms underlying drying, controlled rewetting, and TIPA addition were clarified, providing practical guidance for the valorization of BOF slags as binders.

Key findings can be summarized as follows: Weathering inhibits reactivity: Both WK2 and K3 slags lost nearly all hydraulic activity due to pre-hydration and carbonation during outdoor storage, while the well-preserved K2 remains fully reactive. Drying restores reactivity: Moderate drying at 40 °C effectively removed moisture and unstable hydrates, restoring reactivity in weathered slags to levels comparable with fresh slag. Drying at 105 °C was less effective, likely due to densification or transformation of surface phases. TIPA is effective only in low-lime slag: The grinding aid restored hydration in WK2 by enhancing phase dissolution during milling but was ineffective for the high-lime K3 slag where portlandite and carbonate layers dominated. Controlled rewetting is dosage-dependent: Rewetting dried slags with 0.5 wt.% water reactivated WK2 and partially improved K3, but increasing to 1 wt.% water reduced reactivity, indicating that excess moisture favors renewed passivation. Slag composition governs treatment success: Low-lime slags (K2, WK2) can be fully reactivated by different strategies, while high-lime slags (K3) remain only partially restorable, regardless of treatment. Practical implication: Mild drying combined with moisture management appears the most robust and scalable option for restoring BOF slag reactivity, while grinding aids may be considered as complementary but not stand-alone solutions.

Overall, these findings demonstrate that the valorization of BOF slags as sustainable binders critically depends on controlling storage-induced weathering and applying tailored pre-treatments. This work provides a foundation for developing industrially viable protocols to stabilize slag reactivity and enable its broader use in low-carbon construction materials.
